 Factories shut as Bangladesh garment workers intensify protests over minimum wage

 Edited by Vivek Dubey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 15, 2026, 15:56 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print Garment workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka Bangladesh was rocked by fresh labour unrest on Sunday, with 13 garment factories shutting indefinitely and five others declaring a one-day holiday as workers intensified protests demanding a sharp increase in the minimum wage. The disruption came a day before the government-appointed wage board was scheduled to meet to discuss a revised pay structure. Protesting workers gathered in Gazipur's Konabari and Mouchak areas, prompting police to use tear gas and sound grenades to disperse them. Factory owners said around 50 units across the industrial zone were closed, although production continued at most factories. The workers have been protesting for weeks, demanding an increase in their minimum monthly wage from 12,500 taka (around $100) to 30,000 taka (around $240). "Workers made attempts to gather at different locations this morning, but law enforcement personnel prevented them with their prompt actions and remain deployed at every key point in the industrial area," Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amzad Hossain said. Authorities deployed 13 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh personnel alongside police in riot gear and the elite Special Response Battalion to maintain order and protect factories. Twenty-five executive magistrates were also assigned to oversee security arrangements. What are the workers demanding? Garment workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka, arguing that their current earnings are insufficient to meet rising expenses on food, housing, transport and healthcare. Their protests have centred on the demand for a "living wage to survive". The government formed a Minimum Wage Board on November 1 to recommend a revised pay structure. The board aims to finalise its recommendations by the end of November, with the new wages expected to take effect from December 1. Workers are expected to receive their first salaries under the revised structure in January. The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said its representatives would attend Monday's meeting to submit their proposal, but warned that its participation in subsequent discussions would depend on the situation.  The unrest has raised concerns over export disruptions during the peak production season for spring and summer orders. Factory owners have warned that prolonged shutdowns could delay shipments and lead to cancellations. Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China. The sector employs more than four million workers and accounts for over 80 per cent of the country's export earnings.
